A [MATH: 1,971\,\textrm{ft}^3] load of coal is equally distributed between [MATH: 3] hopper wagons. Using the area model above, find how much coal is loaded into each wagon.

sections.normalized_html:
To find how much coal is loaded into each wagon, we need to calculate [MATH: 1,971 \div 3.]

We need to look at the orange and blue rectangles:

  • Let's first look at the blue rectangle (the one on the left-hand side). Its area is [MATH: 1,800,] and its width is [MATH: 3.] Hence, the length of this rectangle must be [MATH: 1,800 \div 3 = 600.] Let's add this to our model:

  • Now, let's look at the orange rectangle (the one on the right-hand side). Its area is [MATH: 21,] and its width is [MATH: 3.] Hence, the length of this rectangle must be [MATH: 21 \div 3 = 7.] Let's add this to our model:

Now, notice the following regarding the big rectangle:

  • its length is [MATH: 600 + 50 + 7 = 657]

  • its width is [MATH: 3]

  • its area is [MATH: 1,800 + 150 + 21 = 1,971]

Therefore, this area model can be used to represent the following multiplication problem:

[MATH: 1,971 = 657 \times 3]

Writing this as a division problem, we get

[MATH: 1,971 \div 3 = 657.]

Therefore, each wagon is loaded with [MATH: 657\,\textrm{ft}^3] of coal.
